query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short, controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment of a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in low-pressure oxygen (1–10 mbar) at 1000–1100 °C for ~1 hour will form a stable, adherent oxide scale that reduces the subsequent high-temperature mass gain by at least 30% compared to the untreated alloy when exposed to air at 1200–1300 °C for ≥100 hours.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (or as-fabricated) refractory high-entropy alloy containing elements capable of forming protective oxides (e.g., Cr, Al, Ta).
generation.intervention: Controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in a low-pressure oxygen environment at 1000–1100 °C for about 1 hour.
generation.conditions: Following the intervention, the alloy is placed in flowing air at 1200–1300 °C for 100 hours or more (e.g., 1200 °C for 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, dense oxide scale (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3, or mixed CrTaO4-based phases) grown during the pre-oxidation stage.
generation.mechanism: This protective surface layer acts as a slow-diffusion barrier, limiting oxygen transport into the underlying metal and thus suppressing further oxidation during high-temperature service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with as-fabricated samples, pre-oxidized specimens will show at least 30% lower mass gain due to oxidation and improved surface integrity under the specified high-temperature air exposure.
generation.baseline: The untreated alloy, which develops an irregular and less protective oxide scale leading to higher mass gain and earlier onset of accelerated oxidation under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: Sufficient levels of oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr, Al, Ta) in the RHEA are required for a stable scale to form; prolonged or excessively high-temperature pre-oxidation may cause undesirable grain growth or microstructural changes.
generation.uncertainty: Exact mass gain reduction may vary if the alloy’s composition or processing history differs significantly, or if the partial pressure of oxygen during pre-oxidation is not adequately controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two RHEA sample sets of identical composition and processing history. Apply the pre-oxidation treatment (low-P O2, 1000–1100 °C, ~1 hour) to one set, and leave the other as a control. Expose both sets at 1200–1300 °C in flowing air for 100 hours.
measurements: Mass change measurements recorded at intervals throughout the 100-hour heat treatment.
Surface and cross-sectional analysis of the oxide layer by SEM/EDS to characterize oxide scale thickness and microstructure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain (≤10% reduction) or if they fail to form a discernibly more coherent and continuous oxide scale, the hypothesis is falsified.

Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

decision.trend: Earlier work on NbMoCrTiAl (PMC7513042) has shown that adding hard ceramic phases can boost mechanical properties while retaining decent oxidation resistance. More recently, studies of WVTaTiCrx coatings (PMC10142552) have emphasized how chromium promotes a protective oxide layer for improved high-temperature oxidation resistance. However, these approaches relied on bulk or clad-level composition changes. Despite better oxidation performance, fully effective long-term behavior under oxygen-rich environments at temperatures above 1200°C remains challenging, especially without resorting to further alloying additions.
decision.unsolved: A robust solution, not dependent on additional alloying elements, that provides stable and protective surface barriers remains elusive. Achieving efficient oxidation resistance solely through a single, non-alloying intervention—such as a thermal treatment or surface engineering—has not yet been conclusively demonstrated for refractory high-entropy alloys at ultra-high temperatures.
decision.lever: Conduct a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (e.g., in low-pressure oxygen at ~1000–1100°C for ~1 hour) to form a stable, adherent oxide layer on the existing HEA surface.
decision.why: From the observed benefits of forming protective oxide scales in steels and in Cr-containing refractory coatings, a short, controlled high-temperature exposure in partial oxygen can deliberately grow a uniform scale from native alloy constituents without introducing new elemental additions. This approach is particularly applicable for ultra-high-temperature refractory HEAs, limiting further inward oxygen diffusion and enhancing oxidation resistance while avoiding changes to bulk composition.
